supplier_excerpts.quote:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$
For a real function $f$ defined at the nodes, write $I_n f:=I_n(f(x_0),\ldots,f(x_n))$.

For products indexed by $k\ne j$, use the length-$n$ list $\widehat x_{j,k}$ ($0\le k<n$), where $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_k$ for $k<j$ and $\widehat x_{j,k}=x_{k+1}$ for $k\ge j$; the product is in this order and is empty when $n=0$. Strict ordering gives $x_j-\widehat x_{j,k}\ne0$ for every factor, so [[lem-finite-product-of-nonzero-reals-is-nonzero]] and the field inverse law make each $w_j$ well defined.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $k\ne j$, strict ordering of the nodes gives $x_j-x_k\ne0$. The denominator product in $w_j$ is nonzero by [F6], so its inverse $w_j$ exists and is nonzero by [F5]. The product lemma [F2] gives the numerator of $\ell_j$ as a monic polynomial of degree $n$; scaling its coefficients by $w_j$ gives a formal polynomial of degree $n$ with the same evaluation as $\ell_j$, according to the coefficient-list convention [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

1.2 If $i=j$, each factor in $\ell_j(x_i)$ is $(x_j-x_k)/(x_j-x_k)=1$, so $\ell_j(x_i)=1$. If $i\ne j$, the numerator contains the factor $x_i-x_i=0$ while all denominator factors are nonzero, so $\ell_j(x_i)=0$. [given, F1, F5, algebra]

1.3 The product lemma [F2] applied to $x_0,\ldots,x_n$ gives a monic polynomial of degree $n+1$ evaluating to $\omega_n$, with degree and leading coefficient understood from the formal list [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F4]

1.4 If $x$ differs from every node, each factor $x-x_j$ is nonzero by [F5], so the product lemma [F6] gives $\omega_n(x)\ne0$. [given, F1, F5, F6]

2.1 Write each $\ell_j$ by its coefficient vector through index $n$, padding the vector with zeros as in [F3]. For each $k\le n$, take the finite sum of the $k$th coefficients scaled by $y_j$. These coefficients form a vector through index $n$; [F3] supplies a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ evaluating to $\sum_jy_j\ell_j=I_ny$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra, construct] ∎

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

1.1 By [F2], $p:=I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At node $x_i$, [F1, F2] give $p(x_i)=\sum_{j=0}^ny_j\ell_j(x_i)=y_i$. Thus an interpolant exists. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Let $q$ be any formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ with $q(x_i)=y_i$. Extend the actual coefficient lists of $p$ and $q$ by zeros through index $n$, obtaining vectors $(a_k)$ and $(b_k)$; these are vectors for their evaluations, not padded formal objects. The vector $c_k=a_k-b_k$ defines by [F3] a formal polynomial $r$ of degree at most $n$; [F5] gives $r(t)=p(t)-q(t)$ for every real $t$. Since $p$ and $q$ agree at all nodes by step 1.1 and the choice of $q$, $r$ has the $n+1$ distinct roots $x_0,\ldots,x_n$. If $r$ were nonzero, [F4] would give at most $\deg r\le n$ roots, a contradiction. Hence $r$ is the zero formal polynomial; by [F3], every $a_k-b_k=0$. The canonical coefficient lists of $p$ and $q$ are therefore identical, so $p=q$. [given, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 This proves that the interpolant from step 1.1 is the unique formal polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying the node values. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎

interface_reconciliation.node_order: Batch 4 uses x_0<...<x_n. The Chebyshev definition lists x_j=cos(theta_j) with increasing theta_j, hence decreasing x_j. Reindex by x_tilde_k=x_{n-k} and y_tilde_k=y_{n-k}; products and sums are unchanged under the same finite permutation. Batch 19 also proves its cardinal interface directly for its stated ordering.
interface_reconciliation.operator: Supplier I_n y is exactly sum_j y_j ell_j at distinct nodes; batch 19 applies it to y_j=f(x_j).
interface_reconciliation.reproduction: For p of degree at most n, I_n(p(x_0),...,p(x_n)) and p interpolate the same data; thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely proves they are equal. The batch-19 cardinal lemma separately proves I_n^sigma p=p.
interface_reconciliation.uniqueness: The supplier proof uses n+1 ordered, hence distinct, nodes and the at-most-degree-many-distinct-roots theorem for a degree-at-most-n difference.
interface_reconciliation.finite_precision: No finite-precision stability claim is used or imported.
